PAGA PRE-SUIT NOTICE LETTER
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

NOTICE OF ALLEGED VIOLATIONS
This notice is submitted by Jordan Lee regarding Acme, Inc., pursuant to Labor Code § 2699.3.

Aggrieved employee: Jordan Lee
Employer: Acme, Inc.

Specific Labor Code provisions alleged to have been violated: Labor Code § 226(a) (itemized wage statement); Labor Code § 512(a) (meal periods)

Facts supporting each alleged violation: Employees were required to work through rest breaks without additional pay, and timekeeping records show no 10-minute break recorded on multiple shifts.

Legal theories supporting each alleged violation: Failure to provide rest breaks under Labor Code section 226.7, and failure to pay all wages owed under section 204.

PAGA PRE-SUIT NOTICE: CONTENT AND DELIVERY REQUIREMENTS
Before an aggrieved employee may bring a civil action under PAGA (Labor Code § 2699) for most Labor Code violations, Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(1)(A) requires the aggrieved employee or their representative to give written notice by online filing with the California Labor and Workforce Development Agency (LWDA), and by certified mail to the employer, Acme, Inc., of the specific provisions of the Labor Code alleged to have been violated, including the facts and theories to support the alleged violation. Under the current statute, a notice filed with the LWDA under this provision, and any employer response to it, must be accompanied by a $75 filing fee, which is subject to a fee waiver under Government Code §§ 68632 and 68633.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(1)(A), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(1)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.3.)
  "(B) A notice filed with the Labor and Workforce Development Agency pursuant to subparagraph (A) and any employer response to that notice shall be accompanied by a filing fee of seventy-five dollars ($75). The fees required by this subparagraph are subject to waiver in accordance with the requirements of Sections 68632 and 68633 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(1)(B), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(1)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.3.)

Code § 2699.3) — used as evidence of what California's Private Attorneys General Act requires of a PAGA pre-suit notice, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee's situation. PAGA is a distinctly Californian enforcement mechanism; most states have no comparable statute letting a private employee stand in for a state labor agency to pursue civil penalties. The "facts and theories" specificity language quoted above is part of the section's current text (amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026); this research did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-2024 version of the statute, so whether that exact phrase originated with the 2024 reform (AB 2288/SB 92) or predates it is not confirmed here — only that it is part of the section as currently in force. The two citations below are both drawn from the same statutory section (§ 2699.3), subdivisions (a)(1)(A) and (a)(1)(B), rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was located for this specific point beyond it. What counts as sufficiently specific "facts and theories" has been the subject of considerable litigation not reviewed here; this clause states only the statutory text, not how courts have applied it to any particular notice.

WHO QUALIFIES AS AN "AGGRIEVED EMPLOYEE" UNDER PAGA
Labor Code § 2699(c)(1) defines who has standing to bring a PAGA action. As currently written, an "aggrieved employee" is any person who was employed by the alleged violator and personally suffered each of the violations alleged, during the period prescribed under Code of Civil Procedure § 340. A separate, narrower definition applies only to civil actions brought by certain long-standing nonprofit legal aid organizations acting as counsel of record under § 2699(c)(2); for those actions, "aggrieved employee" instead means any person employed by the alleged violator against whom one or more of the alleged violations was committed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699(c)(1), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.)

THE LWDA'S 65-DAY RESPONSE WINDOW
After an aggrieved employee's PAGA notice is filed, Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(2)(A)-(B) gives the LWDA a window to act. If the agency does not intend to investigate, it must notify the employer and the aggrieved employee by certified mail within 60 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice; the aggrieved employee may then commence a civil action once that notice is received, or once 65 calendar days pass from the postmark date of the notice without any agency notice being provided. If the agency does intend to investigate, it must notify the parties of that decision by certified mail within 65 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice, after which it has 120 calendar days to investigate and issue any citation; if no citation issues within these combined periods, or the agency fails to give timely notice, the aggrieved employee may then commence a civil action.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(2)(A), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.3.)

If the agency determines that no citation will be issued, it shall notify the employer and aggrieved employee of that decision within five business days thereof by certified mail. EMPLOYER CURE RIGHTS UNDER THE 2024 PAGA REFORM
California's 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288 and SB 92) created cure processes under Labor Code § 2699.3 that differ by employer size, effective as of § 2699.3's operative date of October 1, 2024. An employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may, within 33 days of receiving the notice, submit a confidential cure proposal to the LWDA for one or more of the alleged violations, triggering an agency-supervised evaluation process. An employer not eligible for that smaller-employer track — because it employed 100 or more employees during the relevant period — may instead, after being served with a PAGA lawsuit, request a court-supervised early evaluation conference and a stay of proceedings. A separate, narrower cure track exists specifically for wage-statement violations of Labor Code § 226(a).

  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(c)(2)(A), Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (c)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.3.)

DEFAULT CIVIL PENALTY AMOUNTS UNDER PAGA
Labor Code § 2699(f) sets the default civil penalty for a Labor Code violation that does not carry its own specifically-provided civil penalty. If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the penalty is $500. If the person employs one or more employees, the general default penalty is $100 for each aggrieved employee per pay period, with several statutory carve-outs: a $25 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies to certain wage-statement violations meeting specific conditions under Labor Code § 226(a); a $50 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where the violation resulted from an isolated, nonrecurring event lasting no more than 30 consecutive days or four consecutive pay periods; and a $200 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where, within the preceding five years, the agency or a court already found the employer's underlying policy or practice unlawful, or where the court finds the employer's conduct was malicious, fraudulent, or oppressive.

HOW A PAGA RECOVERY IS SPLIT BETWEEN THE STATE AND EMPLOYEES
Labor Code § 2699(m) sets the default allocation of civil penalties recovered by aggrieved employees in a PAGA action: 65 percent goes to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency for labor-law enforcement and worker/employer education, and 35 percent goes to the aggrieved employees. A different rule applies to the flat $500 penalty recoverable under § 2699(f)(1), which is not split with employees.

THE ONE-YEAR LIMITATIONS PERIOD FOR A PAGA CLAIM
A PAGA civil action is a statutory penalty action, and Code of Civil Procedure § 340(a) sets a one-year limitations period for an action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture given to an individual, or to an individual and the state — the category a PAGA action falls into — except where the statute imposing the penalty prescribes a different limitation. Labor Code § 2699(c)(1) itself measures "aggrieved employee" status by reference to "the period prescribed under Section 340 of the Code of Civil Procedure," confirming that this one-year period is the operative reference point for PAGA. Separately, Labor Code § 2699.3(e) provides that the time spent in the pre-suit notice and any agency cure-review process is not counted against the time limited for commencing the civil action — that is, the running of the limitations period is tolled while those statutory notice and cure procedures play out.

The quoted text of § 340(a) itself carves out an exception "if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation"; the PAGA statutory text reviewed here (§§ 2699 and 2699.3) was not found to prescribe a different limitations number of its own — it instead cross-references § 340 directly — but this research did not review case law interpreting how the one-year period interacts with a continuing violation, a later-amended PAGA notice, or relation-back to an earlier-filed civil complaint, all of which have been litigated; this clause states only the statutory text, not how courts have applied it.

expectedJSON.body: California's 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288 and SB 92) created cure processes under Labor Code § 2699.3 that differ by employer size, effective as of § 2699.3's operative date of October 1, 2024. An employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may, within 33 days of receiving the notice, submit a confidential cure proposal to the LWDA for one or more of the alleged violations, triggering an agency-supervised evaluation process. An employer not eligible for that smaller-employer track — because it employed 100 or more employees during the relevant period — may instead, after being served with a PAGA lawsuit, request a court-supervised early evaluation conference and a stay of proceedings. A separate, narrower cure track exists specifically for wage-statement violations of Labor Code § 226(a).

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code § 2699(f) sets the default civil penalty for a Labor Code violation that does not carry its own specifically-provided civil penalty. If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the penalty is $500. If the person employs one or more employees, the general default penalty is $100 for each aggrieved employee per pay period, with several statutory carve-outs: a $25 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies to certain wage-statement violations meeting specific conditions under Labor Code § 226(a); a $50 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where the violation resulted from an isolated, nonrecurring event lasting no more than 30 consecutive days or four consecutive pay periods; and a $200 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where, within the preceding five years, the agency or a court already found the employer's underlying policy or practice unlawful, or where the court finds the employer's conduct was malicious, fraudulent, or oppressive.

citations.quote: (f) For all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided, there is established a civil penalty for a violation of these provisions, as follows:(1) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the civil penalty is five hundred dollars ($500).(2) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, the civil penalty is as follows:(A) One hundred dollars ($100) for each aggrieved employee per pay period, except that:(i) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, and the alleged violation is a violation of paragraphs (1) to (7), inclusive, or paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 226, the only civil penalty applicable under this part is twenty-five dollars ($25) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the employee could promptly and easily determine from the wage statement alone the accurate information specified by subdivision (a) of Section 226. If the alleged violation is a violation of paragraph (8) of subdivision (a) of Section 226, the civil penalty applicable under this part for the violation is twenty-five dollars ($25) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the employee would not be confused or misled about the correct identity of their employer or, if their employer is a farm labor contractor, the legal entity that secured the services of that employer. This subdivision does not apply if the employer has failed to provide an itemized payroll statement during any of the pay periods at issue.(ii) The civil penalty is fifty dollars ($50) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the alleged violation resulted from an isolated, nonrecurring event that did not extend beyond the lesser of 30 consecutive days or four consecutive pay periods.(B) The civil penalty is two hundred dollars ($200) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if either of the following are met:(i) Within the five years preceding the alleged violation, the agency or any court issued a finding or determination to the employer that its policy or practice giving rise to the violation was unlawful.(ii) The court determines that the employer's conduct giving rise to the violation was malicious, fraudulent, or oppressive.(3) If the alleged violation is a failure to act by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, there shall be no civil penalty.

A different rule applies to the flat $500 penalty recoverable under § 2699(f)(1), which is not split with employees.

expectedJSON.body: A PAGA civil action is a statutory penalty action, and Code of Civil Procedure § 340(a) sets a one-year limitations period for an action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture given to an individual, or to an individual and the state — the category a PAGA action falls into — except where the statute imposing the penalty prescribes a different limitation. Labor Code § 2699(c)(1) itself measures "aggrieved employee" status by reference to "the period prescribed under Section 340 of the Code of Civil Procedure," confirming that this one-year period is the operative reference point for PAGA. Separately, Labor Code § 2699.3(e) provides that the time spent in the pre-suit notice and any agency cure-review process is not counted against the time limited for commencing the civil action — that is, the running of the limitations period is tolled while those statutory notice and cure procedures play out.

citations.quote: 340. Within one year: (a) An action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture, if the action is given to an individual, or to an individual and the state, except if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation.
(e) The periods specified in this section are not counted as part of the time limited for the commencement of the civil action to recover penalties under this part.
